title: Highest‑Rated Film Ever Expands to 3,200 Theaters, Dominates Box Office Rankings
body:
The documentary “All That Breathes” has become the highest‑rated film in cinema history, and the buzz surrounding its critical acclaim has translated into an unprecedented theatrical rollout. A24 is now distributing the film across more than 3,200 screens in the United States, a scale normally reserved for blockbuster franchises, and the title has already begun to dominate weekend box‑office charts. The move marks a striking reversal for a genre that many industry analysts believed was in permanent decline, and it underscores how a single work can reshape expectations for documentary cinema.

The film’s meteoric rise began on the festival circuit, where it earned a rare perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes and an unprecedented 99 % approval rating on Metacritic. Critics praised its intimate storytelling, masterful cinematography, and the way it weaves personal narratives into larger environmental themes. Those accolades quickly spilled over into social media, where audiences shared glowing reviews and recommended the documentary as a “must‑see” experience. The resulting word‑of‑mouth momentum prompted A24 to expand the release far beyond the limited‑run strategy typical for nonfiction titles.

Historically, documentaries have struggled to secure wide theatrical distribution. Since the mid‑2010s, streaming platforms have siphoned off a large portion of the market, offering filmmakers a guaranteed audience and a modest payout without the logistical challenges of a cinema run. Even highly acclaimed works such as “Amy” or “Free Solo” were confined to a few hundred screens at most. By contrast, “All That Breathes” is being shown in venues ranging from art‑house theaters to major multiplexes, a decision that reflects both confidence in the film’s universal appeal and a strategic gamble by A24 to revive the theatrical documentary model.

Industry insiders see the rollout as a test case for how premium‑priced, critically lauded nonfiction can compete with big‑budget fiction. Box‑office analysts note that the film’s opening weekend gross, while modest compared with superhero releases, is already outpacing the average earnings of recent documentaries by a factor of three. Moreover, the film’s per‑screen average is among the highest for any documentary in the past decade, suggesting that audiences are willing to travel for a compelling nonfiction experience when the marketing narrative emphasizes cultural relevance and artistic merit.

The broader implications extend beyond a single title. If the experiment proves financially viable, studios may reconsider their distribution strategies for documentaries, allocating larger marketing budgets and securing more screens for future releases. This could also encourage filmmakers to pursue more ambitious projects, knowing that a theatrical pathway remains open. Conversely, the success may be an outlier driven by the film’s unique subject matter—a rare glimpse into the lives of urban wildlife caretakers in Delhi—and its timing amid heightened global concern for climate and biodiversity issues.

Looking ahead, the performance of “All That Breathes” will likely influence how the industry balances streaming and theatrical releases for nonfiction content. A strong box‑office run could spark a renaissance of cinema‑first documentaries, prompting festivals, distributors, and exhibitors to collaborate on larger, more coordinated releases. Even if the film eventually migrates to streaming platforms, its initial theatrical triumph will have already demonstrated that critical acclaim can still translate into mass‑audience attendance, reshaping the narrative around documentaries’ place in the modern entertainment ecosystem.
